summary: This Best Current Practice discourages embedding references to unique, globally routable IP addresses in Internet hosts, such as in configuration. It describes the problems that causes and looks at alternatives, such as using names.

eli5.summary: Writing a house number in all your notes becomes a problem when the house moves. Use a name instead. This document explains why.

subtitle: Why hard-coding globally routable IP addresses into products hurts the Internet, and what to do instead.

tldr.problem: Some vendors hard-code globally routable IP addresses, such as a time server, into product firmware, which overloads services, burdens address blocks and creates security risk.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC recommends disabling unused features, giving operators an interface, using domain names or SRV records as service identifiers, using reserved documentation addresses, and discovering local services.
tldr.outcome: It sets out best current practice for vendors and service operators, with an appendix describing a real case of over 700,000 routers pointing at one NTP server.

facts.label: Embedded NTP address in case study

today: RFC 4085 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 105). The unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC.

sections.title: The Practice Being Discouraged
sections.content:
Some vendors of consumer electronics and network gear hard-code globally routable IP addresses in firmware. These are typically individual server addresses or subnet prefixes, used as service identifiers or as subnet identifiers.

The RFC gives two examples: the address of a Network Time Protocol server embedded in the firmware of hundreds of thousands of hosts, and address prefixes once reserved by IANA embedded in a router so it can discard packets with apparently invalid source addresses. The practice probably arose to simplify configuration, but the benefit comes at the expense of others. The RFC reminds readers that using an address as an identifier is temporary.
sections.eli5: Some gadget makers write a fixed internet address inside the gadget. That seems handy, but addresses change owners, so it causes trouble later.

sections.title: The Problems Caused
sections.content:
Embedded addresses make a growing number of hosts depend on a single central service, which can fail when the combined load overwhelms it. This runs against hierarchically deployed services that would otherwise be robust.

The Domain Name System (DNS) provides indirection, letting an operator reconfigure resources or balance load without changing clients. For instance, several DNS records with the same name can be rotated round-robin in successive answers.

Embedded addresses also “taint” the address blocks they sit in. Traffic may keep arriving after a block has been reassigned, which hampers IANA and the registry hierarchy in reallocating blocks. Because consumers cannot be relied on to fix problems, the RFC places responsibility on the manufacturer or vendor.
sections.eli5: If everybody calls the same phone number, that line gets jammed. And if the number is given to someone new, they keep getting calls meant for the old owner.

sections.title: Recommendations for Vendors
sections.content:
Designers should not assume their products live only in the single global Internet they see today. The recommendations are:

  • Disable unused features by default, especially those that generate unsolicited Internet traffic.
  • Provide a user interface for every such feature. For example, a DNS resolver should let the operator set servers or enable an automated protocol such as DHCP. These features should start disabled, and enabling them should alert the operator.
  • Use domain names as service identifiers, in a domain the vendor controls or has permission to use, for example a service-specific prefix like sntp-server.config.example.com. SRV records (RFC 2782) are an alternative, such as a lookup for _ntp._udp.example.com.
  • Use reserved addresses in defaults and documentation: 192.0.2.0/24 for IPv4 (RFC 3330) and 2001:DB8::/32 for IPv6 (RFC 3849). Private addresses from RFC 1918 should not be used for this.
  • Discover local services: providers and enterprises should advertise local services such as NTP, for instance through DHCP (RFC 2132).
  • Avoid publishing service IP addresses: operators of public services should deprecate explicit advertisement of their addresses.

Domain names are not a cure-all. They are also ephemeral and can change owners, so vendors should explore failure modes if control of a domain is lost.
sections.eli5: Instead of a fixed address, give each gadget a name to look up, let its owner change settings, and keep new features switched off until someone turns them on.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
An embedded address often means a host-based trust model, where the host at that address is trusted. Because globally routable addresses are ephemeral, unknown parties may be trusted inadvertently.

The RFC also warns about remote control mechanisms that change a host's configuration without the user's knowledge. If one exists it should be fully disclosed, since malicious parties could exploit it, and it should be disabled by default and enabled or disabled by the user.
sections.eli5: If a gadget trusts whoever lives at a certain address, a stranger who moves in there gets trusted too. Secret remote controls are even riskier, so they should be off unless the owner turns them on.

sections.title: Case Study: The Wisconsin NTP Flood
sections.content:
Appendix A describes the motivating case. In May 2003 the University of Wisconsin found that NetGear had shipped over 700,000 routers whose firmware hard-coded the address 128.105.39.11, also known as ntp1.cs.wisc.edu, a public stratum-2 NTP server.

Because of that embedded configuration and an unrelated bug in the SNTP client, each affected router could send one query per second to that address, producing a large flood of traffic from hundreds of thousands of sources. The RFC says the university, with NetGear's cooperation, would build a new anycast time service to mitigate the damage.
sections.eli5: A company made hundreds of thousands of routers that all asked one university computer for the time, over and over. The university was swamped with questions.
